questions.q: The Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 is broadly divided into two parts. These are:
o: Sections and Rules
Sections (the body) and Orders/Rules (the First Schedule)
Chapters and Articles
Preamble and Schedule only
questions.src: CPC structure — Sections lay down general principles (substantive, harder to amend); Orders and Rules in the First Schedule deal with procedural detail (more flexible)

questions.q: Under Order I of the CPC, when a suit is filed against a wrong party who has no real connection to the dispute, this is called:
o: Non-joinder of parties
Misjoinder of parties
Res judicata
Cause of action
questions.src: Order I CPC — misjoinder is the addition of a party with no relevancy to the suit; the court may strike out such a party

questions.q: When a necessary or proper party is NOT included in a suit, and the court allows their addition on request, this is called:
o: Misjoinder of parties
Non-joinder of parties
Interpleader suit
Set-off
questions.src: Order I CPC — non-joinder is the omission of a relevant party; court may add them on the plaintiff's application

questions.q: The doctrine of Res Judicata under Section 11 of the CPC essentially bars:
o: A court from hearing any civil suit at all
A court from trying any suit or issue that has already been directly and substantially decided between the same parties by a competent court in a former suit
Any appeal from being filed
Only criminal cases from being reopened
questions.src: CPC Section 11 — bars re-litigation of matters directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, decided by a competent court

questions.q: The doctrine of Sub Judice under Section 10 of the CPC applies when:
o: A case has already been finally decided
A matter is directly and substantially in issue in a previously instituted suit between the same parties, still pending in a competent court — the later suit must be stayed
A party wants to withdraw a suit
There is a dispute about court fees
questions.src: CPC Section 10 — bars trial of a suit where the same matter is already pending (sub judice, 'under judgment') in an earlier-instituted suit between the same parties

questions.q: Territorial jurisdiction of a civil court is primarily determined by which of the following (among others)?
o: The plaintiff's personal choice of any court in India
Where the defendant resides/carries on business, or where the cause of action wholly or partly arises
The amount of court fee paid
The plaintiff's place of birth
questions.src: CPC Sections 16-20 — territorial jurisdiction generally based on defendant's residence/place of business or where the cause of action arises

questions.q: 'Cause of action' in a civil suit refers to:
o: The court fee payable on the suit
The bundle of essential facts which the plaintiff must prove to be entitled to the relief claimed
The name of the presiding judge
The limitation period applicable
questions.src: Settled CPC concept — cause of action is the set of facts giving rise to the right to sue; essential for determining jurisdiction and limitation

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of the essential grounds a plaint must generally establish, according to standard pleading practice?
o: Jurisdiction of the court
Cause of action
Court fee paid
The defendant's personal opinion of the plaintiff
questions.src: A plaint must establish jurisdiction, cause of action, limitation compliance, and court fee — the defendant's personal opinion is irrelevant to plaint drafting

questions.q: Under Order VII, when can a plaint be rejected by the court?
o: Only if the defendant requests it
Where it does not disclose a cause of action, or the relief claimed is undervalued and not corrected, or it is insufficiently stamped and not corrected, among other specified grounds
Only after the trial has concluded
Never — a plaint can only be withdrawn, not rejected
questions.src: Order VII Rule 11 CPC — grounds for rejection of plaint include no cause of action disclosed, insufficient court fee/valuation not corrected, and suit barred by law

questions.q: A 'set-off' in a written statement refers to:
o: A counter-suit filed separately
A defendant's claim of a sum of money against the plaintiff that can be adjusted against the plaintiff's claim in the same suit, provided conditions under Order VIII are met
A request to transfer the case
An application for condonation of delay
questions.src: Order VIII Rule 6 CPC — set-off allows a defendant to claim adjustment of a liquidated, ascertained sum against the plaintiff's claim within the same suit

questions.q: A 'counter-claim' by a defendant, as distinguished from a set-off, is:
o: Identical to a set-off in every respect
An independent claim by the defendant against the plaintiff which can extend beyond merely answering the plaintiff's claim, effectively giving the defendant the status of a plaintiff for that claim
Only permitted in criminal matters
Not permitted under the CPC at all
questions.src: Order VIII Rule 6A CPC — counter-claim is broader than set-off; defendant can claim independent relief, not limited to a mere adjustment

questions.q: Under Order VI Rule 17 CPC, amendment of pleadings by a party is:
o: Never permitted once a suit is filed

Permitted at any stage of proceedings, on such terms as may be just, if necessary for determining the real question in controversy between the parties — subject to the proviso restricting amendments after trial has commenced absent due diligence
Automatic without court permission
Only permitted for the plaintiff, never the defendant
questions.src: Order VI Rule 17 CPC — court may allow amendment at any stage if necessary for determining the real controversy; the 2002 proviso restricts post-trial-commencement amendments unless the party could not have raised the matter earlier despite due diligence

questions.q: When a defendant, despite being duly served with summons, fails to appear on the date fixed for hearing, the court may:
o: Automatically dismiss the suit
Proceed ex-parte against the defendant and decide the case on the material available
Wait indefinitely for the defendant
Refer the matter to arbitration compulsorily
questions.src: CPC Order IX — where defendant fails to appear despite due service, the court may proceed ex-parte

questions.q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a 'decree' from an 'order' under the CPC?
o: There is no legal difference between the two terms

A decree is the formal expression of an adjudication conclusively determining the rights of parties on the matters in controversy in the suit; an order is a formal expression of any decision of a civil court which is not a decree
An order is always appealable, but a decree is never appealable
A decree only applies to criminal matters
questions.src: CPC Section 2(2) defines 'decree'; Section 2(14) defines 'order' — decree conclusively determines rights of parties on matters in controversy, order is any other formal decision

questions.q: Under the CPC, 'execution' of a decree refers to:
o: The process by which the court delivers judgment
The legal process by which a decree-holder enforces or gives effect to the judgment/decree obtained from the court, to actually obtain the fruits of the decree
Filing a fresh suit on the same cause of action
An application to condone delay in filing an appeal
questions.src: CPC Order XXI governs execution — the machinery by which a decree-holder realises the benefit of a decree (e.g., through attachment and sale of property, arrest and detention, etc.)

questions.q: Which of the following is a recognised mode of execution of a money decree under the CPC?
o: Attachment and sale of the judgment-debtor's property
Automatic transfer of the judgment-debtor's bank account without court order
Public shaming of the judgment-debtor
Criminal prosecution of the judgment-debtor as the sole remedy
questions.src: CPC Order XXI — recognised modes of execution include attachment and sale of property, arrest and detention in civil prison (in limited circumstances), and appointment of a receiver

questions.q: A 'temporary injunction' under Order XXXIX of the CPC is granted to:
o: Permanently resolve the dispute between parties
Preserve the subject matter of the suit or maintain status quo during the pendency of litigation, to prevent irreparable harm before the final decision
Award final compensation to the plaintiff
Replace the need for a full trial
questions.src: Order XXXIX CPC — temporary injunctions are interim reliefs to preserve the status quo/subject matter during the pendency of the suit

questions.q: Under Section 80 of the CPC, before instituting a suit against the Government or a public officer in respect of an act purporting to be done in their official capacity, a plaintiff must generally:
o: Obtain prior permission from the Supreme Court
Serve a notice in writing, and normally wait for a specified period (generally two months) before filing the suit, except where urgent interim relief is sought with leave of the court
File the suit directly without any notice
Pay double court fees
questions.src: CPC Section 80 — mandatory notice requirement before suing Government/public officers, with a statutory waiting period, subject to court's discretion to grant leave for urgent interim relief

questions.q: Under Order XXXIII of the CPC, a suit filed 'in forma pauperis' (by an indigent person) allows:
o: The plaintiff to avoid paying court fees upfront if they satisfy the court of their inability to pay, with fees potentially recoverable from the proceeds if the suit succeeds
Automatic dismissal of the suit
Only government employees to file suits
The defendant to claim indigent status, not the plaintiff
questions.src: Order XXXIII CPC — permits an indigent person to institute a suit without upfront payment of court fees, subject to the court's satisfaction on the applicant's means

questions.q: An 'appeal from an original decree' under the CPC lies to which court, ordinarily?
o: The same court that passed the decree
The court to which appeals ordinarily lie from decisions of the court which passed the decree (i.e., the next higher/appellate court)
The Supreme Court directly in every case
No appeal is possible from an original decree
questions.src: CPC Sections 96-99A (Appeals from Original Decrees) — appeal lies to the appellate court in the hierarchy above the court that passed the decree

questions.q: A 'review' under Section 114 and Order XLVII of the CPC is:
o: An appeal to a higher court

An application to the SAME court that passed the decree/order, asking it to reconsider its own decision on specified limited grounds (e.g., discovery of new evidence, error apparent on the face of the record)
Automatically granted upon request
Only available in criminal cases
questions.src: Order XLVII CPC — review is made to the same court on limited grounds; distinct from an appeal (which goes to a superior court)

questions.q: A 'revision' under Section 115 of the CPC is generally available to the High Court in respect of:
o: Any decree passed by any subordinate court

Cases decided by a subordinate court where no appeal lies, and the High Court finds the subordinate court exercised jurisdiction not vested in it, failed to exercise jurisdiction vested in it, or acted illegally/with material irregularity
Only criminal matters
Only cases involving the Government
questions.src: CPC Section 115 — revisional jurisdiction of the High Court, confined to jurisdictional errors or illegality/material irregularity, in cases where no appeal lies

questions.q: Under Section 3 of the Limitation Act 1963, if a suit, appeal, or application is filed after the prescribed period of limitation, the court:
o: May allow it if the other party does not object
Shall dismiss it on the ground of limitation, even if the defence of limitation has not been specifically raised by the opposite party
Must always condone the delay
Has no power to dismiss it
questions.src: Limitation Act 1963, Section 3 — mandatory bar; court must dismiss a time-barred suit/appeal/application even if limitation is not pleaded as a defence

questions.q: Section 5 of the Limitation Act 1963, which allows condonation of delay on 'sufficient cause', applies to:
o: Suits, appeals, and applications equally
Appeals and applications, but NOT suits (with a further exclusion for certain applications under Order XXI of the CPC)
Only suits, not appeals or applications
Only criminal proceedings
questions.src: Limitation Act 1963, Section 5 — explicitly excludes suits from its scope, and also excludes applications under Order XXI CPC (execution); confirmed by multiple legal sources including legalserviceindia.com, lawbhoomi.com

questions.q: In Collector, Land Acquisition, Anantnag v. Mst. Katiji (1987), the Supreme Court held that the term 'sufficient cause' under Section 5 of the Limitation Act should generally be interpreted:
o: Strictly and narrowly, to discourage any delay whatsoever
Liberally, in a justice-oriented manner, since a litigant does not ordinarily stand to benefit by delaying and refusing condonation can defeat a meritorious case on mere technicality
Only in favour of government litigants
It should never be condoned regardless of cause
questions.src: Mst. Katiji (1987) — settled leading case establishing the liberal, justice-oriented approach to condonation of delay; consistently cited across multiple current legal sources
